**Session Notes: Cofounder Buyout Decision**

**The Situation**
Founder running a bootstrapped company with a 50/50 cofounder (actually 55/45 split). Two major accounts represent 60% of revenue, and the cofounder holds the personal relationships with both CEOs. The cofounder has been coasting for months — three-week holiday during launch, poor sales documentation, minimal Slack responsiveness. The founder is carrying most of the operational load and is deeply frustrated.

**The Actual Tension**
This isn't a binary "good partner vs. bad partner" problem. The founder needs the cofounder *out* (operational clarity, decision speed, end to daily friction). But the cofounder is also the *only person holding the two relationships that fund the company*. Buying him out removes the friction but *directly trades into* the thing keeping the founder awake at night — loss of those account relationships.

The founder initially framed this as an unsolvable hostage situation. I pushed back on that framing. He pushed back harder — correctly — pointing out that a structured 90-day retainer with earnout tied to renewal actually *does* solve the hostage problem. He was right. The constraint I thought was absolute turns out to be manageable.

Once that constraint moved, the decision simplified: this is about operational clarity, not about account risk. He's already running the company solo; the cofounder isn't adding anything but friction. The buyout just makes official what's already happening in practice.

**The Decision**
Buying out the cofounder's 45% equity stake with a structured transition.

**Terms discussed (not yet finalized with cofounder):**
- Fair-market valuation on 45% (founder will get an independent valuation before bringing a number to the table)
- 90-day retainer post-equity close
- Account handoff milestones in months 1-2 (warm customer intros, founder takes primary contact)
- Earnout tied to renewal on the two major accounts (so cofounder has skin in them staying)
- Hard cutoff at day 90

**Why he chose it**
Operational simplicity and speed. The cofounder is checked out. Two years of conversations haven't changed that. The founder is already doing the work; buying the equity just removes the overhead of managing around a non-present partner. The retainer structure solves the account vulnerability that initially looked like a blocker.

**What he's accepting — the real cost**
This is crucial: he knows the cost but hasn't fully internalized it yet.

He's accepting that he becomes the only person making decisions, the only stakeholder in the outcomes, the only person in the room when things break. No cover. No peer judgment. A single point of failure on the entire company.

Those two big accounts (60% of revenue) will have a new primary contact. Even with a solid transition plan, they're more fragile. The cofounder's personal relationships with those CEOs existed over years; the founder's will be brand new. The accounts will probably stay — especially with the earnout incentive — but this isn't risk elimination, it's risk transformation.

The founder has intellectually accepted this. He articulated it clearly: "you're accepting a structural vulnerability — you become a single point of failure on decisions, customers, everything. That's the price of operational clarity."

But he hasn't yet *felt* what that means day-to-day. He will, around month 2-3 after the cofounder is gone, when a customer problem hits and there's no one to loop in, no one who owns it alongside him.

**What to watch if he returns**
If he returns, the buyout will likely have closed or be in final negotiation. The questions will probably be: (1) the transition is harder than expected — accounts are stickier to the cofounder than planned, or the handoff is taking longer, (2) he's feeling the weight of being alone at the top and wondering if he made a mistake, or (3) the cofounder is being difficult on the way out.

The first two are predictable; the third depends on how the negotiation goes.

If he wobbles on the decision itself, remind him: he accepted this knowingly. The cost was named. The accounts are probably staying (you can check against the earnout trigger if they're not). The cofounder was checked out; solo he's doing better work. This is the trade he made. The trap is thinking he could have had both — full operational clarity *and* a resilient stakeholder in the room. That's not available. He chose clarity.

The real work starts after the cofounder is gone: diversify those account relationships so they don't live on him alone, build other revenue streams so 60% concentration doesn't own him, get actual operational systems in place so he's not carrying it all in his head. Those are the problems the buyout didn't solve. Those are what matters next.

This also does something else: it stops the 4am spiral dead. Anxiety lives in abstraction. The moment you're in an actual conversation with those customers, talking about their roadmap and what they need, you move from "will they leave?" to "here's what matters to them and how we're going to serve it." That's a completely different nervous system state.
